what inclusion means: making sure the mix actually participates, with employees accepted and treated fairly (working definition, attributed; diversity without inclusion is the honest gap)

claims.claim: Diversity at work is the mix of identity-based differences among and between people — including race and ethnicity, gender, sexual orientation, and age — that affect their lives as applicants, employees, and customers; this is the working definition used in the lesson, attributed to OpenStax's Principles of Management (section 12.1).

Inclusion is the degree to which employees are accepted and treated fairly by their organization, and it is one way companies demonstrate that they value diversity; this working definition is attributed to OpenStax's Principles of Management (section 12.1).

The business case for diversity introduced by Taylor Cox and Stacy Blake and summarized by OpenStax (section 12.3) lists six opportunities for companies that value diversity: cost advantages, improved resource acquisition, greater marketing ability, system flexibility, and enhanced creativity and better problem solving.

Organizations perceived to value diversity attract a larger applicant pool — studies show women and minorities have stronger job-pursuit intentions toward employers that promote workplace diversity in recruitment — and organizations with a visible climate of diversity experience lower turnover among women and minorities (OpenStax 12.3).

In the United States, the EEOC enforces federal laws that make it illegal to discriminate against a job applicant or an employee because of race, color, religion, sex (including pregnancy, transgender status, and sexual orientation), national origin, age (40 or older), disability, or genetic information; most employers with at least 15 employees are covered (20 in age-discrimination cases), and the laws apply to hiring, firing, promotions, harassment, training, wages, and benefits.

Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 makes it an unlawful employment practice to fail or refuse to hire, to discharge, or to discriminate against any individual in compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment because of race, color, religion, sex, or national origin; the EEOC was created by Title VII (EEOC statute text; corroborated by OpenStax 12.4).

Diversity initiatives carry real challenges: research summarized by OpenStax (12.4) found that as work-group diversity increased, White employees and male employees sometimes felt less attached to the organization and were more likely to leave, and employees can misunderstand diversity programs — so inclusion must be actively managed rather than assumed.

Unconscious bias shows up in real workplace decisions: people automatically feel comfortable with those who think, act, and look like them, and that subjective comfort — often discussed as 'fit' — can override objective qualifications in hiring and promotion (SHRM, 'Putting Humanity into HR Compliance').

Diversity management refers to organizational actions that aim to promote greater inclusion of employees from different backgrounds into an organization's structure through specific policies and programs; best practices include commitment from top management, identifying new talent pools, and creating safe avenues for dialogue such as employee resource groups (CFI).

conflictingEvidence: The business case (diversity improves talent, decisions, and markets; OpenStax 12.3) coexists with honest counter-evidence: diversity programs can lower organizational attachment and raise turnover intentions among some majority-group employees when not managed well (OpenStax 12.4), and a diverse headcount alone does not show that employees are actually included. The lesson treats both as one honest picture: the mix is worth pursuing, and it only works when inclusion is actively built.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Management, Section 12.1: An Introduction to Workplace Diversity
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook). Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-22 (openstax.org serves the page to a browser user-agent). Supplies the lesson's attributed working definitions: diversity as identity-based differences among and between two or more people that affect their lives as applicants, employees, and customers (race and ethnicity, gender, sexual orientation, age); inclusion as the degree to which employees are accepted and treated fairly by their organization, a way companies demonstrate they value diversity; surface-level diversity (visible characteristics such as age, body size, visible disabilities, race, or sex) vs deeper differences; identity groups. Used as reference only; facts restated in original prose.
